summary.text: A galaxy merger can happen when two or more galaxies collide, and it is the most violent type of galaxy interaction.
In a merger, stars lose their orderly orbits and end up on random, interacting orbits, which is what is seen in elliptical galaxies.
Mergers also set off extreme star formation, then leave the galaxy with little gas to make new stars.

items.prompt: Two disk galaxies collide. Before the merger their stars circle in orderly paths. What do the stars' orbits look like afterward?

options.label: Even tidier paths all within one flat disk
A complicated, random network, as in elliptical galaxies
Two separate families of stars that never mix
Straight lines passing right through the center

items.explain: The ordered motion is converted into random energy, and the resulting galaxy is dominated by stars on random, interacting orbits like elliptical galaxies.

items.prompt: Stars almost never get close enough to collide in a merger. Where does the burst of new stars come from?

options.label: Old stars crash together and break into new ones
Dark matter turns into stars near the center
Black holes shed clumps of matter that become stars
Giant molecular clouds fall inward and collide, forming stars

items.explain: Giant molecular clouds rapidly fall to the center, collide with other clouds, and the collisions induce condensations into new stars.

items.prompt: A galaxy merged with another a few billion years ago and now has few young stars. Why?

options.label: The merger used up most of its gas, so star formation was quenched
Its young stars were thrown out of the galaxy
Its dark matter blocks new stars from forming
Its older stars have swallowed the young ones

items.explain: Major mergers use up the majority of the gas, so further star formation after the merger is quenched.

items.prompt: Astronomers cannot observe a merger rate directly. What do they often use as a stand-in?

options.label: The total number of stars inside each galaxy
The brightness of every single galaxy's nucleus
How many galaxies in a sample sit close together
The orbital speed of the galaxy's outermost stars

items.explain: Since the merger rate is impossible to observe, close pair fractions are often used as a proxy.

items.prompt: Computer simulations based on Hubble data follow the Milky Way meeting Andromeda. What do they predict for the result?

options.label: They pass through and return unchanged
The two fuse into one elliptical galaxy
They fuse into a larger spiral galaxy
They fly apart as stars scatter

items.explain: Simulations indicate that the galaxies will finish fusing under gravity into one elliptical galaxy.

items.prompt: Why do astronomers care about how often galaxies merge?

options.label: It shows how galaxies grew into their current forms
It shows how quickly the universe has cooled
It tells us how many stars end up colliding
It tells us how much dust each galaxy contains

items.explain: The merger rate is a fundamental measurement of galaxy evolution and gives clues about how galaxies grew into their current forms.

paragraphs.heading: When galaxies collide
paragraphs.text: A galaxy merger can happen when two or more galaxies run into each other. It is the most violent way galaxies interact. Gravity, and friction between their gas and dust, reshape the galaxies involved. The exact result depends on things like the angle and speed of the collision and the galaxies' sizes and make-up, and it is still a very active research topic.

paragraphs.heading: Why mergers matter
paragraphs.text: How often galaxies merge is a basic measure of how galaxies evolve. It also gives clues about how galaxies grew into their present forms over long stretches of time. Astronomers run computer simulations of mergers to learn more about how galaxies form.

paragraphs.heading: Violent relaxation
paragraphs.text: As two galaxies approach, the stars and dark matter in each are affected by the other. Late in the merger, gravity changes so fast that stars lose all trace of their old orbits, a process called violent relaxation. Two disc galaxies start with their stars circling in an orderly way in two flat discs. The merger turns that orderly motion into random motion, leaving a galaxy whose stars follow a tangle of random orbits, which is what we see in elliptical galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Bursts of new stars
paragraphs.text: Mergers also set off huge amounts of star formation. Stars almost never actually hit each other, but giant clouds of molecular gas rush to the centre and smash into other clouds, which makes them condense into new stars. A major merger can produce thousands of Suns' worth of new stars a year, though typical mergers make fewer than 100. Our own galaxy makes only about two new stars a year.

paragraphs.heading: Running out of gas
paragraphs.text: All this violence leaves a merged galaxy with little gas for making new stars. A few billion years after a major merger, the galaxy has very few young stars left. That is what today's elliptical galaxies look like, with very little molecular gas and very few young stars. The stage when star formation has been shut off like this is called the post-starburst phase.

paragraphs.heading: Our galaxy and Andromeda
paragraphs.text: A well-known simulation models a merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda. Simulations based on Hubble data suggest that two billion years after they collide, the two galaxies will have fully fused. The result will be a single elliptical galaxy, much like those common in the nearby universe.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to catch in the act
paragraphs.text: Telling whether two galaxies are merging, have merged or will merge can be difficult. Sometimes it is even hard to know whether they are interacting at all, because some mergers have no obvious features. Since the merger rate cannot be observed, astronomers often use a stand-in: the fraction of galaxies in a sample that are close to one another.
